title: What a Burst Pipe Does to a House Over Days | Gold Water Fire, Phoenix, AZ
description: A day-by-day look at what a burst pipe does to a house when nobody is home, what to check first when you walk in, and what usually has to be dried or rebuilt.
h1: What a Burst Pipe Does to a House Over Days When Nobody Is Home
breadcrumbLabel: Burst Pipe While Away From Home
intro: You unlocked the door after a week away and the air was wrong before you saw anything. Warm, heavy, with a smell like a wet basement in a house that does not have one. Maybe the carpet gave under your shoe in the hallway. Maybe the ceiling in the living room has a stain shaped like a country. Whatever went wrong went wrong while you were gone, quietly, with nobody there to hear it, and standing in the doorway trying to understand how far it went is a genuinely disorienting place to be.

sections.heading: How the damage builds, hour by hour and day by day
sections.body: Water damage is not one event. It is a sequence, and each stage makes the next one worse. Knowing roughly where a house is on that timeline helps you understand what you are looking at when you walk in, and why a small visible stain often means a much larger wet area behind it.

cards.heading: The first hours
cards.body: Water leaves the pipe and follows gravity and the path of least resistance: down through the subfloor, along floor joists, into wall cavities. Drywall wicks moisture upward from the bottom plate. Carpet pad soaks and holds. At this stage almost nothing looks dramatic. A supply line under a sink or a washing machine hose can push a lot of water in an hour, and most of it goes somewhere you cannot see.

cards.heading: Day one to two
cards.body: Materials that absorbed water start to swell and separate. Laminate flooring buckles at the seams. Engineered wood cups. Baseboards pull away from the wall. MDF cabinet toe kicks turn spongy. Drywall paper starts to hold moisture even after the surface feels dry to the hand. Humidity in the closed house climbs, which means dry rooms far from the leak start absorbing moisture out of the air.

cards.heading: Day two to four
cards.body: Microbial growth generally begins in this window when materials stay wet and the air stays humid. That is where the musty smell comes from, and it is a smell that shows up before visible growth does. Paint bubbles. Ceiling drywall sags if water pooled on top of it. Insulation in wall cavities compresses and stops drying on its own.

cards.heading: Day five and beyond
cards.body: Now it is structural and cosmetic at the same time. Growth spreads across the back of drywall and into carpet backing. Wood framing that stayed saturated can start to soften. Cabinet boxes delaminate. In a house that was closed up with the air conditioning off, high heat and high humidity together speed all of this up considerably, which is a real factor in the Phoenix area during summer.

sections.heading: What to do in the first thirty minutes after you find it
sections.body:
None of this requires special equipment and none of it has to be perfect. It just slows the damage down while you figure out the rest.

Find the main water shutoff and turn it off. In most Arizona homes it is at the street side of the house near the hose bib, or in a box near the sidewalk. If you cannot find it, shut off the individual angle stops under the fixtures you can reach.

If water is anywhere near an outlet, a panel, or a light fixture, do not stand in it. Turn off power to that area at the breaker if you can reach the panel without walking through water, and if you cannot, leave that alone and stay out of the room.

Take photos and video before you move anything. Wide shots of each affected room, then close ups of the flooring, baseboards, ceilings, and the source if you can see it. Insurance conversations go much better with a record made before cleanup starts.

Open interior doors and closet doors and turn the air conditioning on. Moving, conditioned air helps. Fans pointed at wet drywall help a little. Neither one dries a wall cavity, but they buy time.

Move what you can save: rugs, boxes on the floor of a closet, anything paper or upholstered sitting on wet flooring. Set it somewhere dry, not in a pile.

sections.heading: Why the wet area is almost always bigger than the stain
sections.body: This is the part that surprises most people. Water travels sideways under flooring and inside walls, so the visible mark is the end of the story, not the whole of it. A stain on a ceiling means water crossed a joist bay to get there. Wet baseboard in one room usually means the bottom plate and the cavity behind it are wet in the next room too. Restoration work relies on moisture meters and thermal imaging to map the actual boundary of the wet area, then targeted drying with air movers and dehumidifiers to pull moisture out of framing and subfloor rather than just off the surface. The reason that matters is simple: if a wall is closed back up while the cavity is still holding moisture, the smell comes back, and so does the growth, months later, after the new paint is on. Surface dry and structurally dry are not the same thing, and only one of them is the goal. Our page on water damage restoration walks through how that drying process is actually run.

sections.heading: What usually has to be replaced, and what usually does not
sections.body: Not everything wet is lost. Solid wood framing, tile over concrete, and most hard surfaces can often be dried in place. Sealed cabinet boxes sometimes survive. Hardwood can sometimes be saved depending on how long it was wet and what is under it. What typically does not come back: carpet pad, wet insulation, MDF and particleboard, and drywall that sat saturated at the bottom of a wall. Those get cut out, usually in a clean horizontal line a foot or two up, because the cut is cheaper and more certain than trying to dry material that will hold moisture regardless. That cut is also why a water loss turns into a construction project. Once drywall, baseboard, flooring, and cabinetry are out, someone has to put the house back: hang and texture drywall, match paint, reinstall trim, set flooring, rebuild the cabinet run. Having drying and rebuilding handled by the same people means the person who opened the wall is the person who closes it, and nothing gets lost between two companies pointing at each other. That side of the work is covered on our reconstruction and rebuild page. If you would rather just have someone look at it with you and tell you what you are dealing with, that is a fine place to start. You can reach Gold Water Fire at (480) 999-3339 or Help@goldwaterfire.com, or through the contact page.

faqs.q: How long can a house sit wet before it becomes a mold problem?
faqs.a: As general guidance in the restoration industry, microbial growth can begin on wet materials within roughly two to three days when moisture and warmth are both present. Heat and a closed up house speed that along. This is not a reason to panic if you have been gone longer than that, growth is treatable, but it is the reason drying gets started rather than scheduled for next week.

faqs.q: The floor looks dry now. Do I still need anything done?
faqs.a: Probably yes, and it is worth checking rather than assuming. Surfaces dry long before the material underneath does. Carpet can feel dry while the pad below it is saturated, and drywall can look fine while the bottom eight inches are still wet inside. A moisture meter reading takes a few minutes and either confirms you are fine or shows you where the water actually went.

faqs.q: Should I call my insurance company before or after I call a restoration contractor?
faqs.a: Either order works, and many people do both the same day. Sudden and accidental water releases like a burst supply line are commonly covered, while long term seepage often is not, so the distinction in your policy matters. Document everything with photos before cleanup begins, keep any piece of failed pipe or hose, and write down when you left and when you returned.
